newsitem.title: BELARUS: International concern grows over Belarus turmoil.
newsitem.headline: International concern grows over Belarus turmoil.

text.p: International concern was growing on Tuesday at a bitter power struggle between parliament and president in the former Soviet republic of Belarus.
Both the United States and members of the North Atlantic Assembly have taken the side of parliament in its fight with President Alexander Lukashenko.
Lukashenko has been trying to change the constitution to boost his powers in a referendum that ends on Sunday.
His critics accuse him of trying to set up a dictatorship and members of parliament said on Monday they had started impeachment moves against him.
"The United States believes that it's a crisis that's causing, in fact, some damage in the political system," State Department spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters in Washington.
"There does not appear, in our view, to be any legal basis in the Belarus constitution for the action that President Lukashenko has been taking," Davies said.
In Paris, members of the North Atlantic Assembly also ranged themselves behind parliament.
Assembly president Karsten Voigt of Germany told a news conference that Lukashenko's behaviour was "illegal, non-democratic and sometimes even crazy".
The assembly groups parliamentarians from 40 European and North American countries including the 16 NATO states.
President Lukashenko looked more isolated on Tuesday after the resignation of a key ally but vowed to press on with the controversial referendum.
Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir, who had remained loyal to Lukashenko during months of political paralysis, stepped down on Monday.
Lukashenko named deputy prime minister Sergei Ling as acting premier. Labour minister Alexander Sosnov also resigned.
About 200 anti-Lukashenko demonstrators kept up a vigil outside parliament through the night, fearing an attempt by security forces to dissolve the assembly by force.
Deputies invited the president to attend Tuesday's session but Lukashenko told state television late on Monday that time for compromise was fast running out.
"If the people's deputies do not understand my appeal (to stop attacking me and back the referendum) then we will have to meet and go our separate ways once and for all," he said.
It was not clear whether he meant by this he planned to move against the parliament, his opponents' stronghold.
Deputies said Chigir, a well-respected figure in this former Soviet republic of 10 million, had resigned because of Lukashenko's refusal to cancel his referendum.
In his television interview Lukashenko made clear that he had no plans to shelve the poll, which he hopes will grant him new powers and extend his term by more than two years.
"I am saying for the last time -- it is time to understand the train has already left. It will not be stopped, the referendum will happen," he said.

If the constitutional court approves the deputies' impeachment moves, 132 members of parliament would have to vote in favour of the decision. Only 108 deputies, including some who back Lukashenko, attended Monday's session.
Lukashenko's top aide, Vladimir Zametalin, told Reuters the president could stop parliament impeaching him even if the constitutional court approved such a decision.
"The president of the republic will use the maximum possibilities available to him to get out of the situation without conflict," Zametalin said in a telephone interview.
Asked if this could include dissolving parliament and the constitutional court, he said: "It's entirely possible. The president has many options."
